intro:
The best law firm logos are simple, typographic and built for trust. Most leading firms use a wordmark of the firm's name in navy or black, with no scales, gavels or columns. The ones you remember add one ownable detail: a coloured box, a monogram, an underline or a single accent colour.

What makes a good law firm logo?

Clarity first: a client should recognise the firm before they have to decode a symbol. That is why so many firms shorten long partnership names, like Skadden, Sidley, Milbank and Fenwick.

One distinctive detail: Skadden's red box, Dentons' purple arrow, Hogan Lovells' lime square and Fish & Richardson's teal dot make otherwise simple wordmarks memorable.

A tone that fits the practice: Wall Street firms look like private banks, tech law firms like Cooley and Fenwick look like the startups they advise, and litigation boutiques often choose bolder, more personal type.

Below are 54 law firm logos in six groups: New York's elite firms, global giants, the London Magic Circle and UK firms, tech, startup and IP firms, litigation boutiques and design-led firms (including Fox Berman, a firm I branded), and international firms. Each logo has a slide with my handwritten notes and a short explanation. For more professional services brands, see my investment firm logos, private equity logos and bank logos, and my guide to logo colours.

logoResearch.name: Cravath
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Cravath, Swaine & Moore traces its roots to 1819 in New York and is one of the oldest firms on Wall Street.
observations: Wide, classical capitals in navy feel like an engraving on a stone building.
Shortening the full partnership name to one word made the firm easier to say and remember.

logoResearch.name: Paul Weiss
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison was founded in New York in 1875.
observations: The two names sit in a navy square, like a seal or an app icon.
The comma after Paul keeps a trace of the long partnership name.

logoResearch.name: Sullivan & Cromwell
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Algernon Sullivan and William Nelson Cromwell founded the firm in New York in 1879.
observations: Small serif capitals feel formal and traditional.
The ampersand joins the two founders, the classic law firm formula.

logoResearch.name: Davis Polk

listIntro: The boards below show all 54 law firm logos in one consistent format, grouped into New York's elite firms, global giants, London and UK firms, tech and IP firms, litigation boutiques, and international firms.
Each logo is reviewed for its design decisions, not for the size, rankings or reputation of the firm.
sectionNames: London Magic Circle and UK firms
Tech, startup and IP law firms
sectionIntroductions: Wall Street's oldest firms use classic serif and small-capital wordmarks, with one or two bold exceptions like Skadden's red box.
The largest global firms are more willing to use colour, shapes and monograms, because their logos have to work in dozens of countries.
London's Magic Circle mixes tradition and boldness, from Slaughter and May's quiet purple to Linklaters' magenta and Freshfields' heavy capitals.
Firms that advise startups and technology companies look like tech brands, with bold sans serifs, icons and bright accents.
Trial boutiques use more personal, distinctive type, because their partners are the brand.
International firms combine local languages and scripts with simple, global-friendly wordmarks.
sectionBridge: This is a visual comparison of law firm logos, not a ranking of law firms.
Look at how each logo uses type, colour and one detail to signal trust, scale or specialism.
entryFallbacks: The identity relies on a few clear decisions to stay recognizable.
Notice how the logo would look on a letterhead, a court filing and a website.

findings.heading: Shorter names win
findings.text: Skadden, Sidley, Milbank, Fenwick, Freshfields and Cleary Gottlieb shorten long partnership names, which makes the logo easier to say, remember and use.

findings.heading: One accent beats a symbol
findings.text: Skadden's red box, Hogan Lovells' lime square, Dentons' purple, Linklaters' magenta and Fish & Richardson's teal dot do more than any scales of justice.

findings.heading: Navy and serif still dominate
findings.text: Cravath, Davis Polk, Kirkland & Ellis, Simpson Thacher and Garrigues use the classic language of serif type and dark colour to signal stability.

findings.heading: Tech law firms look like tech
findings.text: Cooley, Fenwick, Goodwin, Orrick and Wilson Sonsini use modern sans serifs and icons that feel familiar to startup founders.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for a law firm logo
checklistItems: Is the firm name easy to read on a letterhead, a court filing and a phone screen?
Is there one ownable detail, like a colour, box, monogram or underline?
Does it avoid generic legal clichés like scales, gavels and columns?
Does it fit your practice, from Wall Street finance to startups or family law?
Will it still work in one colour, embossed on stationery or engraved on a door plate?

faq.question: What makes a good law firm logo?
faq.answer: A good law firm logo is easy to read, distinctive, and flexible. Most of the strongest examples lead with the firm’s name, use one or two restrained colors, and add one ownable detail, such as an oversized letter, a monogram, or a single accent color.

faq.question: What colors are best for a law firm logo?
faq.answer: Navy and black are the most common because they read as serious and print well on documents. The most memorable firms pair that base with one accent they use consistently, such as Susman Godfrey’s red, Fox Berman’s tropical orange, or Mills & Reeve’s purple.

faq.question: Should a law firm logo use scales of justice or a gavel?
faq.answer: Usually not. None of the 54 logos in this article uses scales, a gavel, or a column. Those symbols signal “law” in general but say nothing about your firm, so a distinctive wordmark or monogram is usually stronger.

faq.question: Should a law firm logo use a serif or a sans-serif font?
faq.answer: Both work. Serifs feel established and formal, while sans-serifs feel direct and modern. Spacing, weight, and one distinctive letterform matter more than the category.

faq.question: Should I use a symbol or a wordmark?
faq.answer: A wordmark is often the clearest foundation because it makes the firm name memorable. Add a monogram or symbol when you need a compact mark for favicons, social avatars, and signage.

faq.question: How much does a law firm logo cost?
faq.answer: Logo marketplaces start at a few hundred dollars, and branding agencies often charge $25,000 to $100,000 or more for a full identity. At Ebaq Design, a complete law firm brand identity costs $3,000 flat and is delivered in one week, guaranteed.

faq.question: How long does it take to design a law firm logo?
faq.answer: With a focused process, a logo and core identity can be designed in one week. At Ebaq Design, the brand identity is delivered in one week, guaranteed, and a website follows in one to two more weeks.
